Caricature

KAIR-ih-kuh-chur -- four syllables, stress on the first syllable, KAIR. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Caricature is a comically distorted portrayal of a person's most distinctive features.

Boardwalk artists will sketch your caricature in five minutes, oversized ears and all.

Worked Example

In history class, the students study an 1870s magazine cartoon of a railroad tycoon. The man's actual gold watch chain has been drawn as thick as a ship's anchor chain, and his top hat rises taller than the locomotive behind him -- one glance tells you exactly how rich and self-satisfied the artist thought he was.

The cartoon is a caricature: it takes one specific person's real, recognizable features -- the watch chain, the hat, the smirk -- and blows them far past life size for comic and critical effect. A caricature always has a particular target; the joke lives in the gap between the real face and the inflated one.

How Caricature Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

distortion

distortion: a twisted, overblown version of something

cartoon

cartoon: a humorous drawing

mockery

mockery: an act of making fun of someone

Antonyms

likeness

likeness: a faithful, accurate image of someone

realism

realism: showing things exactly as they are

How Strong Is It? — cartoon → distortion → caricature

cartoon vs. caricature

cartoon vs. caricature: Cartoon says only that a drawing is humorous -- it may invent its subject entirely and mean no harm.

distortion vs. caricature

distortion vs. caricature: Distortion is the strongest of the three: a caricature bends real features for a laugh, but calling a portrayal a distortion accuses it of twisting the truth itself out of shape.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of caricature.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — caric-

root — caric-: to load, to overload (Italian caricare, from Late Latin carricare 'to load a wagon,' from carrus 'cart')

suffix — -ature

suffix — -ature: action or result of (as in signature) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Italian caricare meant 'to load,' rolling back to Latin carrus, 'cart,' and -ature names the result of an action, as in signature -- so a caricature is literally 'an overloading.' The artist piles more and more onto the subject's most distinctive features until the portrait is comically overloaded.

Root Check

Word Choice

A caricature targets ONE SPECIFIC person or thing and inflates its real, recognizable features, usually in a drawing or description. Keep it apart from its unit-mate spoof, which humorously imitates a whole work, genre, or style -- a spoof copies the format of cooking shows; a caricature inflates the host's eyebrows. The word also stretches figuratively: a trial run so unfairly that reporters call it 'a caricature of justice' -- a distorted, unrecognizable version of the real thing.
